items.title: Show HN: OnKey – I'm a bad singer, so I built an app to show where I'm off-key
items.body:
Hi all I was pretty terrible at singing, now I’d say I’m bad but not terrible. This is because I’ve been using a singing app (won’t name it here) that scores me on my pitch and timing throughout the song so that I can improve. Lately however, the app I’ve been using has flooded their song list with songs that aren’t originals. I didn’t like this at all as for me, it’s easier to try to improve when you’re singing along to the original. So, I asked an agent (Claude Code) if it could write some code to listen to Spotify and also listen to me and see if it could detect both pitches and score me. It impressed me by writing some Python and showing me my pitch in the terminal! It couldn’t go all the way though and detect the singer’s pitch in real time. So I found the next best setup and built OnKey, a Mac app that needs to listen to the song once (it doesn’t save it) and then when it’s learnt the song (takes a couple of minutes), you can sing along to the pitch track that it’s learnt. OnKey is free to use and open source under the MIT license. It can listen to Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube playing in your browser with the right permissions. During the build I found that someone had done something similar in Nightingale, but this requires a library of songs exported to disk and who has this in 2026 (maybe some of you ;) - but we need to help the normies too). You can check out a demo video on the site of me singing (warning given) here: https://singonkey.app The app sends out to

comment (wnissen): What a fun idea! I love that the song doesn't have to be programmed in by the developer. Will give it a try. Have you played the Rock Band and similar "rhythm games" that were all the rage in the Wii era? I don't know that it helped my singing per se but gave some incentive to practice. In case anyone is interested, you can test your relative pitch perception (as opposed to producing the pitch) in this excellent Yale site: https://www.themusiclab.org/quizzes/td I got 15th [sic] percentile!
comment (nopurpose): Didn't know that external apps can interact with Youtube in a tab in Safari. Looks nice, I sing so badly that I never dare to try if not alone. items.title: mihirgupta0900/tv-home: Debloat a slow, ad-filled Android TV over Wi-Fi and give it a fast Apple TV-style home screen. One prompt for Claude Code, or do it by hand.
items.body:
# tv-home

**Make a slow, ad-filled Android TV fast and clean again.** Debloat it over Wi-Fi and give it a
tiny Apple TV-style home screen with rotating nature wallpapers. You can hand the whole thing to
Claude Code with one prompt, or do it by hand with the scripts here.

On a 2 GB TCL Google TV this disabled 25 bloat apps and cut the home screen's memory use from
192 MB to 83 MB. Everything is reversible: packages are disabled, never uninstalled.

## Do it with Claude Code (easiest)

1. On the TV: Settings → System → About → press OK on **Build** 7 times → back → Developer options
   → turn on **USB debugging**. Keep the TV on, on the same Wi-Fi as your computer.
2. Clone this repo, open Claude Code inside it (so it can reuse the launcher and scripts), and paste:

   ```text
   My Android TV is slow and full of ads. Find it on my Wi-Fi, connect over ADB, and debloat it:
   disable the manufacturer's ads, telemetry and junk (reversibly, never uninstall), asking me first
   about apps and features I might use. Then build and install a fast, minimal Apple TV-style home
   screen with a dock of my favourite apps and rotating nature wallpapers. Back up before changing
   anything, check every step with screenshots from the TV, and give me a restore script.

   Heads-up from people who've done this: use the adb-shell Python package if macOS blocks adb; on
   Google TV also disable com.google.android.tungsten.setupwraith or it hijacks the Home button; and
   test the Home button from inside an app.
   ```

3. Accept "Allow USB debugging?" on the TV when asked, then answer a few questions: which apps you
   use, which go in the dock, whether you want wallpapers.

The prompt is short on purpose; Claude works out the details. The gotchas below are there in case it gets stuck.

## Do it by hand (macOS)

```bash
./setup.sh                                                  # Python ADB client, JDK 17, Android SDK
tools/find-tv.sh                                            # finds the TV, saves its IP
tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/tv.py --probe                # model, Android version
tools/disable.sh examples/tcl-google-tv-g07/debloat.txt     # or your own list, see examples/
launcher/build-and-install.sh                               # build + install the launcher
```

Undo everything with `tools/restore.sh  `.

## What's here

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| [PROMPT.md](PROMPT.md) | The prompt for Claude Code / any coding agent |
| [launcher/](launcher/) | The home screen. 4.7 MB including the wallpapers; plain Android, no network, no background services |
| [launcher/res/values/config.xml](launcher/res/values/config.xml) | Dock apps, hidden apps, Live TV app, grid columns |
| [tools/tv.py](tools/tv.py) | Pure-Python ADB client: shell, batch, screenshots, chunked APK push |
| [tools/find-tv.sh](tools/find-tv.sh) | Finds Android TVs on your Wi-Fi |
| [tools/type.sh](tools/type.sh) | Type into the TV's on-screen keyboard from your laptop (`tools/type.sh` alone prompts hidden, for passwords) |
| [tools/disable.sh](tools/disable.sh), [tools/restore.sh](tools/restore.sh) | Apply / undo a debloat list |
| [examples/](examples/) | Debloat lists per TV model |

## The launcher

- Clock, greeting and date top-left. Frosted pills top-right for **Inputs** (HDMI/AV/Live TV
  dropdown; the remote's Menu key opens it too), **Wi-Fi** (shows the network name) and **Settings**.
- A dock of your favourite apps. The focused app's name appears above it over a glow

items.title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
items.body: Tool-using language model agents rely on environmental facts to decide whether an action is permitted. When a tool response omits a safety-relevant fact, an agent may carry out a prohibited action even though the user request is benign and every returned statement is true. We introduce \bench{}, an executable benchmark for evaluating unsafe execution, safety boundaries, and evidence recovery in LLM agents under missing evidence. It contains 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains. By systematically suppressing critical facts, the benchmark measures unsafe execution under critical evidence omission and determines the minimum observed failure cardinality, including failures with full evidence and cases with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. An independent audit tool tests whether agents seek missing facts and then withhold prohibited actions while completing permissible tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial variation across the ten models in omission robustness, evidence acquisition, and appropriate action. Resistance to missing evidence does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all ten models, but agents differ in whether they actively obtain the missing facts and use them to act appropriately in both worlds.

meta.description: MCP server and open registry for HTTP 402 agent payments: decode L402, x402 and MPP challenges and choose a payment rail.

items.body:
# 402MCP.org

The MCP server and open registry for **HTTP 402 agent payments**.

When an AI agent receives `402 Payment Required`, 402MCP tells it which scheme
the server speaks (L402, x402 or MPP), what is being asked for, and exactly how
to pay and retry. When a developer is choosing how an agent should pay, or how an
API should charge agents, it recommends a rail from stated requirements. Behind
both sits an open registry of sourced, scored payment solutions.

- **Site:** https://402mcp.org
- **Remote MCP endpoint:** `https://402mcp.org/api/v1/mcp` (streamable HTTP)
- **npm:** [`@402mcp/mcp`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@402mcp/mcp) (stdio)
- **Install guides:** https://402mcp.org/docs#install

## Install

Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http 402mcp https://402mcp.org/api/v1/mcp
```

Any stdio MCP client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf and others):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "402mcp": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@402mcp/mcp"] }
  }
}
```

## MCP server

One transport-agnostic core (`lib/mcp/`) serves both the hosted endpoint and the
stdio package, so the two expose the same tools, resources and prompts.

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `decode_402_challenge` | Decode a 402 response (L402 macaroon and BOLT 11 invoice, x402 v1/v2, MPP) into exact next steps and the retry header |
| `recommend_payment_rail` | Filter by role, asset, custody, infrastructure, network, scheme, MCP support and maturity; re-weight the criteria; explain every exclusion |
| `search_402_solutions` | Search the registry with filters |
| `get_solution` | One entry in full, with sources and code samples |
| `get_scheme_reference` | Wire format of L402, x402 or MPP |
| `probe_402_support` | One GET to a public URL to see whether it speaks 402. Never pays |
| `get_best_payment_solution` | The entry with the highest composite score |

Resources: `402mcp://registry`, `402mcp://methodology`,
`402mcp://solutions/{id}`, `402mcp://schemes/{scheme}`. Prompts:
`choose_payment_rail`, `handle_402_response`. Every tool is annotated
`readOnlyHint`.

**Safety.** Everything in a 402 response is server-controlled, so the decoder
lists those fields in `untrusted_fields` and never repeats their text as
instructions. It flags expired challenges and macaroons that commit to a
different payment hash than their invoice. The probe refuses private, loopback,
link-local and metadata addresses (including hostnames that resolve to them) and
non-web ports, and the hosted endpoint rate-limits it per client. No tool can
spend money.

## Machine interfaces

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /api/v1/mcp` | MCP (JSON-RPC 2.0, streamable HTTP) |
| `POST /api/v1/decode` | Decode a 402 response |
| `GET /api/v1/recommend` | Recommend a rail from requirements |
| `GET /api/v1/probe?url=` | Probe a URL for 402 support (rate limited) |
| `GET /api/v1/solutions` | Versioned list (`?q=`, `?id=`, `?view=full`) |
| `GET /api/v1/registry` | Canonical feed with ETag / 304 support |
| `GET /api/v1/schemes/{scheme}` | Wire format of L402, x402, MPP |
| `GET /api/v1/status` | Daily liveness of every entry's docs and website |
| `GET /api/v1/changelog` · `/changelog.xml` · `/changelog` | Changes and corrections |
| `/schema/v1/registry.json` · `/schema/v1/solution.json` | JSON Schemas (draft 2020-12) |
| `/openapi.json` | OpenAPI 3.1 |
| `/llms.txt` · `/llms-full.txt` | Plain-text indexes |
| `/.well-known/402.json` · `api-catalog` · `mcp/server-card.json` · `agent-

items.title: rossark0/rossark-motion-skill: Turn any SVG into a professional 60 fps animation. A Claude Code skill that brings anything drawn to life: live faces, full-body acting and whole scenes, in React Native and SwiftUI.
items.body:
# Motion For Anything You Draw

For designers and engineers who want to bring their apps and drawings to life.

Making a drawing move is easy. Making it feel alive is hard: it has to breathe, look around, blink, shift its weight and act, without ever freezing or jumping. This skill helps your agent get there.

It started as the method I used to bring the illustrations in my app to life, and grew into a way to animate anything drawn: characters and creatures, plants, cloth, fire, smoke, water, weather, lights, machines, icons, logos, charts and whole scenes.

The animation above is drawn and animated entirely in code, with the templates in this repo.

## Install

```bash
npx skills@latest add rossark0/rossark-motion-skill
```

## Why use it?

Agents don't animate like animators.

Ask an agent to bring a character to life and it will often swap one drawing for another, so the face teleports from one expression to the next. It moves through each pose with its own eased tween, so the body stops dead at every pose. Everything moves in sync, like a machine. Blinks are so short they flicker, everything bounces, and a thin line shows across the face where two shapes meet.

All these small things add up, and the result looks like a slideshow instead of something alive.

This skill lists those mistakes and how to fix them: one clock for the whole scene, parts that turn around their real pivots, trailing parts that follow a beat later, idle life that never stops, smooth paths through key poses, small amplitudes and strong curves. When you have a reference video, it measures the motion frame by frame before building, because what makes a reference feel alive is often too small to see.

For motion in an interface, it follows [Emil Kowalski's](https://github.com/emilkowalski/skills) rules and Benji Taylor's [Family values](https://benji.org/family-values).

## Reference

- **[SKILL.md](./SKILL.md)**: The skill. Principles, recipes for every kind of subject, live faces, full-body acting, scenes that tell an action, motion in an interface, pitfalls, working from a reference video, and a workflow.
- **[MOTION.md](./MOTION.md)**: A notes file for your project. Copy it next to your art and fill in Part 2 as you go: where the code is, your rules, what your art can't do, and how you check changes. The skill reads it first.
- **[motion.ts](./templates/react-native/motion.ts)** and **[Motion.swift](./templates/swiftui/Motion.swift)**: The engine, for React Native and SwiftUI. Loop and one-shot clocks, `track`, `flow` (smooth acting through key poses), `seg`, `wave`, `loop`, `bell`, `seeded` and the curves.
- **[liveFace.tsx](./templates/react-native/liveFace.tsx)** and **[LiveFace.swift](./templates/swiftui/LiveFace.swift)**: Live eyes and mouths that glide, blink and smile. You give them the geometry and the colours.
- **[sheet.sh](./tools/sheet.sh)**: Contact sheets of a video at its full frame rate, to study timing or check your own render.
- **[track_edges.py](./tools/track_edges.py)**: Measures a subject's edges frame by frame, to catch motion too small for the eye: a 2% jiggle, a float, a sway.
- **[sample_colors.py](./tools/sample_colors.py)**: Reads exact colours from a video frame.
- **[demo/](./demo)**: The scenes on this page, a phone frame and an offline renderer that turns them into MP4 and GIF.

## Demos

**Reveal** ([source](demo/RevealScene.swift), [MP4](demo/reveal.mp4)), at the top of this page. Full-body acting in a phone frame, on one cloc

items.title: Training Small Language Models for Transferable Tool Selection
items.body: As LLM agents operate over corpora of more than ten thousand tools, selecting the right tool for a complex multi-step user instruction becomes a central bottleneck. Tool descriptions cannot all fit in context, and relevance-based retrievers only rank tools without knowing which are actually needed. Recent work instead leverages proprietary commercial LLMs like Claude or ChatGPT to drive a retriever, decomposing the instruction and selecting over retrieved candidates. We show that a small, open model can be trained via reinforcement learning to perform the same functionality. On ToolBench, a Qwen3-8B model post-trained with our recipe outperforms Llama-4-Maverick (402B). In addition, the trained model transfers directly to different retrievers and generalizes to new tool corpora in different domains.

items.title: How Model Context Protocol (MCP) actually works
items.body:
# How Model Context Protocol (MCP) actually works
# Google Cloud Tech
# https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cGuyrANVi4A

[00:04] If you've ever tried to make an AI model, talk to your tools or your data, you've probably realized something. It's messy. Every API behaves differently, every integration needs custom code, and every time the model changes, your connection breaks. The model context protocol, or MCP, was created to fix exactly that. By the end of this video, you'll understand what the model context protocol actually is, why it exists, and how it's changing the way models interact with the world. We'll walk through the core ideas step by step,
[00:39] see how it compares to traditional APIs, and talk about what this means for developers, building agents, or AI powered applications. So what is the model context protocol. At its core, MCP is an open standard for connecting models to tools, data, and context in a really consistent and structured way. You can think of it as a shared language between models and the systems around them. It defines how a model can discover available tools, ask for information, and perform actions without having to know the specific implementation
[01:14] details behind each one. This protocol was introduced by Anthropic and is now being adopted across the industry because it solves one of the biggest pain points in AI development today. How to make models use external resources safely and reliably. So here's why that matters. APIs were never designed for AI models. They were designed for programs that already know exactly what they want, programs that can form precise, deterministic requests. A language model doesn't work that way.
[01:47] It generates text probabilistically. It reasons about uncertain inputs and often needs to ask questions, clarify or explore before it knows what to do. MCP bridges that gap. It gives models a structured way to discover and describe the resources they can use. So things like functions, data sets, documents or prompts are all available through a consistent interface. Instead of hard coding every integration, the model can now dynamically query what's available, use it, and even
[02:21] chain multiple tools together, so all while staying within a safe, standardized framework to understand how MCP actually works, let's unpack the main idea. The protocol defines two sides clients and servers. The client is usually the language model or the agent system that wants to perform a task, something like Cloud, Gemini app or an agent built on top of OpenAI or Google's frameworks. The server is the environment that exposes resources that the model can use a database, a file
[02:56] system, a company's internal tools or even a document search engine. When the client connects to the server, the server doesn't just respond with data. Instead, it advertises what capabilities it supports, what resources exist, what actions can be taken, and what inputs are required. This means the model doesn't need to be pre-programmed with every API or every endpoint. It can dynamically discover them. The communication between these two sides happens through a really simple and well-defined schema.
[03:31] The client sends requests like list available resources, call this action, or retrieve this data. The server then responds with a structured JSON describing what's possible and what happened. That's the essence of MCP, a standardized way for models to talk to their environment. Now let's go a bit deep
[transcript continues in field-notes/staging/cGuyrANVi4A.txt]

items.body:
Octocrawl 

 
   One link. Web data, ready.  
  Markdown and data from web pages, for AI agents and RAG. 
  Fewer tokens than raw HTML. Every result records how it was read.
 

 
     
     
     
     
     
 

 
    Website   ·
    Docs   ·
    Connect MCP   ·
    Blog   ·
    Changelog  
 

---

**Scrape pages. Crawl websites. Turn web content into usable data.**

Octocrawl is an open-source web scraping and crawling toolkit for AI agents, RAG and research. Collect documentation for a knowledge base, extract product details for comparison, or turn web tables and listings into data for analysis. Each page comes with a source record.

[Try a page in your browser](https://octocrawl.dev/?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=top), or [connect your agent](#quick-start) through hosted MCP or the [REST API](https://api.octocrawl.dev). No installation or API key is needed to try the hosted service.

## What can you do with Octocrawl?

| Capability | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| **Scrape a page** | Readable Markdown for LLM context, plus HTML, links, image URLs and page metadata. Request a screenshot on the browser lane. |
| **Map a website** | Discover URLs from sitemaps and page links, and filter them by a search term to find the pages you need. |
| **Crawl a site or section** | Follow links from a starting URL and collect each page's content, with path filters, depth and page limits. |
| **Scrape a list of URLs** | Submit a batch, retrieve results as they arrive, and keep the outcome of every URL, including failures. |
| **Extract structured data** | Get tables and repeated listings as JSON and CSV, or pass a JSON Schema for supported fields such as product names, prices and page labels. [Extraction guide](docs/json-extraction.md). |
| **Read dynamic pages** · local actions | Render JavaScript, click controls, scroll, load more items and follow pagination before extracting content. [Browser actions](docs/scrape-options.md#actions). |
| **Read PDF reports** | Extract a PDF's text layer with page markers for citations. CSV, JSON and plain-text URLs also return their text. [File support](docs/files.md). |
| **Revisit sources on a schedule** · local workers | Run Monitors and send their events to an HTTPS endpoint with retried delivery. [Monitor setup](docs/monitors.md). |

Hosted Octocrawl offers **scrape and map**, and with an account **crawl and batch jobs** (up to 500 pages a crawl, 1,000 URLs a batch); keyless requests use HTTP, and an account key enables the browser lane. Run locally for larger jobs, page actions and Monitors; see [Running Octocrawl](docs/local-setup.md) for setup and self-hosting options. The [web preview](docs/public-preview.md) is a single-page trial, with five pages a day and up to 20 named fields.

## Why Octocrawl?

- **Web data inside your agent.** Connect Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode or Codex through MCP, or build with REST, TypeScript, Python and the Vercel AI SDK.
- **Structured fields without a model by default.** Read supported values from the page itself, with field evidence and explicit missing values. Model fallback is opt-in.
- **Know when a scrape fell short.** Checks flag challenge pages, wrong content, missing facts, truncation and too little content. Blocked and failed results carry a reason; fetched error pages keep their status and Markdown. [Result states](docs/scrape-options.md#failure-results).
- **Trace results back to their sources.** Each page carries an [Evidence Record](apps/pu

items.title: Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents
items.body:
Hi HN! We’re Srikar and Kevan, founders of Alter – https://alterauth.com/ . We’re building access control for agents that can take actions on behalf of multiple users. If you’ve built an internal agent people use through Slack, you may have experienced this scenario: everyone signs in with their own account, but the agent connects to the CRM or billing system with one shared API key, so the agent can do anything that the key can do. User-level authentication in Slack does nothing to control what the agent can do in an external system like the CRM or billing system. Here’s what Alter does: -It acts as a proxy and manages downstream credentials for every API request that an agent takes; -It takes identity into account for every action the agent does. Automatically take into account the end user identity of the person that the agent is taking actions on behalf of. -It enforces fine grained runtime policies and records compliance grade audit logs. Here’s a demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ZqPU14ipGE We started this because we saw first hand how hard it is to build agents in regulated industries. To unlock the true benefits of agents we need to allow agents to take actions, sometimes actions on behalf of end users. I (Srikar) was working at Goldmans and I saw how prohibitively expensive it was for me as a developer to write my own custom auth to enable multi-tenancy in agents and to allow agents to have strict policy controls as they act on behalf of end users. My co-f
comment (souvik1997): Looks cool! One aspect of multi-user agent security, which I think is underexplored, is how context from a higher-privileged session might "leak" into a lower privileged session. Suppose the CEO of a company uses your shared openclaw agent and the agent writes sensitive data (investor emails, for example) to its memory. My understanding is this is not protected by Alter. Then a contractor uses the same agent and can read that same memory. It seems to me that a better agent harness for this kind of multi-user use case is needed; the standard ones like openclaw and claude code simply are not des
comment (avikonduru): How do you handle permissions when the downstream service only offers a shared API key? For example, two sales reps can use the same CRM endpoint but should only access their own accounts. Does Alter check record ownership, or does the developer still need to supply that logic?
comment (mauvehed): That website is literally a vibe-coded template.. How can we put any trust into the app itself?
